recycled-wool.origin: Recycled wool is keratin fiber recovered from existing wool products rather than shorn from sheep. Inputs range from clean pre-consumer waste, such as spinning waste, knitting offcuts and cutting-room clippings, to post-consumer garments sorted by fiber and color. In industry, mechanical fiber recycling is applied mostly to natural-polymer fibers, including wool and cashmere, and to cotton and man-made cellulosics; one Spanish spinner, Hilaturas Ferre, operates plants for recycling post-industrial wool and polyester. Because inputs vary, recycled wool is often blended with virgin fibers to restore length and strength.
recycled-wool.structure: Chemically the fiber is unchanged wool keratin: alpha-helical keratin filaments in a sulfur-rich matrix cross-linked by disulfide bonds, wrapped in overlapping cuticle scales. Research on separating wool from nylon carpet waste has shown that gentle processing can preserve wool's scale structure and tensile strength close to those of virgin fiber. What changes is the physical profile. Tearing and garneting break fibers, so recycled wool has a shorter, more variable length distribution, more broken ends and some dust, and it keeps the dyes, finishes and treatments of its previous life. Mixed inputs bring residues of other fibers, such as polyester or elastane, into the new yarn.
recycled-wool.process: Collected textiles are sorted by fiber content and color, often manually and with growing use of near-infrared scanning; buttons, zips, labels and other hard points are removed, and some lines cut waste into clippings and eject pieces with trims using cameras. The material is opened by pickers and pulled apart on a Garnett or tearing line into loose fiber. Lubricants applied before shredding can reduce fiber damage. Because color is retained, careful shade sorting can avoid redyeing. The fiber is blended, often with virgin wool or synthetic staple, carded and respun into yarn, or processed into felts and nonwovens.
recycled-wool.performance: Recycled wool keeps wool's moisture absorption, warmth and resilience, but shorter fibers give more hairiness, lower yarn strength and more pilling unless the fiber is blended or densely constructed, which suits it to coats, blankets, felts and heavier knitwear. Because it retains its scales, it can still felt and shrink in hot, agitated washing unless an earlier shrink-resist finish survives. Quality depends on the input: clean, sorted pre-consumer waste gives better fiber than mixed post-consumer streams, and mechanical recycling cannot be repeated indefinitely because each pass shortens the fibers further.
recycled-wool.identify: Burn tests are indicative only; recycled wool burns like other wool, smoldering with a burning-hair smell and leaving crushable dark ash. Microscopy shows ordinary wool scale patterns, often with more broken ends, short fibers and mixed colors within one yarn, and may reveal stray synthetic or cellulosic fibers from mixed inputs. No routine laboratory test proves that a wool fiber was recycled, so claims rest on purchase and production records and transaction certificates. FTIR or solubility tests can quantify contaminating fibers in the blend.
recycled-wool.labeling: Under the Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 (15 U.S.C. 68 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 300, US labels must disclose wool and recycled wool separately by percentage of weight. The Act defines recycled wool as fiber returned to a fibrous state from wool that was woven or felted into a product never used by a consumer, or from wool products a consumer did use. Descriptors implying newness, such as virgin wool, are reserved for wool never reclaimed. EU labels follow Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, and recycled content is commonly certified under the Global Recycled Standard or Recycled Claim Standard.
recycled-wool.past: Reclaiming wool is far older than circular-fashion language. The nineteenth-century trade in shoddy, fiber torn from wool rags, supplied cheap cloth, and the US Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 reflected the trade's concern to separate reclaimed wool from new fleece so buyers could tell them apart. The statutory recycled category still groups unused manufacturing waste with worn goods, unlike the pre-consumer and post-consumer vocabulary of voluntary standards. Current research adds chemical and biological separation: keratinase enzymes can digest the wool out of wool-polyester blends to recover clean polyester, and mild acids can dissolve nylon 6 out of wool carpet waste.
